title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 12: What I Learned at Far Eastern University
keywords: What I Learned at Far Eastern University
National Union of Students of the Philippines (NUSP)
the things that money cannot buy
primary_topics: Chapter 12 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- CJP's FEU commencement address on receiving the degree of Doctor of Laws, honoris causa, in which he takes as his theme 'what I as a student imbibed at FEU' and names four lessons: a desire for academic excellence, a craving for a well-rounded education, a search for his Catholic faith, and a hunger for leadership.

His account of a poor boyhood and a near-lost education -- a father who was 'an underpaid but overworked government employee,' the deaths of both parents before he could graduate, and the FEU scholarship, bible-selling and sibling support that carried him to a degree in 1960.

His argument that excellence in one profession is not enough -- that judges and lawyers must be more than 'walking encyclopedias of the Constitution, the codes and judicial doctrines' and need working knowledge of the humanities, economics, sciences and technology to decide modern litigation.

His testimony that FEU, though nonsectarian, gave him his faith through Fr. Michael Nolan and Fr. James Sheehy, and his exposition that spiritual laws carry consequences just as human and physical laws do, with salvation available 'by repentance, restitution and reformation.'
sub_topics: He thanks President Edilberto C. de Jesus and board chair Dr. Lourdes Reyes Montinola for the honorary doctorate, and jokes that with this second honoris causa degree he can at last be 'the academic equal of my wife and children,' having suffered 'a venial inferiority complex' as the only one in the family without a graduate degree.

He recalls his own FEU Institute of Law graduation 42 years earlier in 1960, his father's care for four children and seven siblings, and his father's insistence that education was the key to life even though he never finished college.
He recounts how FEU 'came to my rescue' with a scholarship after his father died, how he sold bibles and textbooks to support himself, and how his mother died during his senior year at law school.

First lesson -- academic excellence: he had wanted UP but could not afford the bus fare to Diliman, enrolled grudgingly at FEU, and found professors 'unusually strict and demanding,' naming Dean Francisco M. Africa, Dr. Benito F. Reyes, Prof. Angelica P. Mendoza and Prof. Rosario P. Melchor, whose logic and grammar he still uses.

Dean Jovito R. Salonga became his role model, gave him 'UP-style education but Harvard and Yale techniques as well,' called on him to recite at the height of his student-activity years, and by constant monitoring of his grades pushed him to graduate with honors and place among the bar topnotchers.

He credits Salonga with recruiting a faculty of future Senate Presidents, Supreme Court justices and Court of Appeals justices who 'demanded excellence, diligence and hard work,' which is why FEU law graduates regularly topped the bar.

Second lesson -- well-rounded education: Dean Alejandro R. Roces preached liberal education under the battlecry 'Education for Culture,' made FEU a center for the arts, became CJP's NUSP adviser and his wedding Ninong in 1961, and was later named the youngest secretary of education under President Diosdado Macapagal.

He quotes FEU President Teodoro Evangelista that education aims to prepare for work 'not as an end in itself but as a means to the enjoyment of life of the mind and spirit,' and translates the philosophy into legal terms: lawyers need the arts, sciences and technology, a breadth that has let him decide cases involving 'avant-garde sciences, new economic paradigms and ultramodern technology.'

Third lesson -- Catholic faith: a product of public schools with 'no catechetical background,' he was recruited by FEU chaplain Fr. Michael Nolan into the FEU Student Catholic Action and taught the rudiments of Catholicism, while Fr. James Sheehy urged him to 'be a Christ for others.'

He lays out a parallel between human, physical and spiritual laws -- contracts and crimes carry damages and jail, gravity carries a fall, and transgressing the Ten Commandments or the Beatitudes damns the spirit -- with salvation as the counterpart of reparation.

Fourth lesson -- leadership: once 'very shy and timid,' he was elected FEUCSO president as a sophomore and co-founded and led the NUSP, encouraged by owners and administrators such as board chairman Don Angel Palanca and treasurer Hector del Rosario, 'Mang Etoy.'
He concludes that these four lessons made him 'the equal of the UP, the Ateneo or the La Salle student' and able to compete with the best from any school in the world.

He reports researching present-day FEU and finding its leaders have continued and improved the old policies -- citing de Jesus's March 9, 1996 installation pledge for a faculty measured by 'the critical thinking they provoke,' the revived FEU auditorium, Dean Andres Bautista's upgrading of legal education, and FEU student Margarita Eugenia F. Victorino's win in the Supreme Court's nationwide essay contest.

He closes by compressing the four lessons into one teaching from Dean Salonga: that beyond the necessities money can buy, 'it is far more important to aspire for the things that money cannot buy, like integrity, honor, dignity and a reverential regard and love for God.'

notable_anecdotes: The venial inferiority complex: he jokes that as the only member of his family without a graduate degree -- a wife with two master's degrees and five children with Ivy League diplomas -- the honorary doctorate finally makes him their academic equal.

The 15-centavo bus fare: granted a UP tuition scholarship, he could not take it because he could not afford the fare from Sampaloc to Diliman, so he 'grudgingly enrolled at FEU which was a walking distance from our home.'

Selling to survive: after his father died, he sold bibles to his professors and textbooks to his classmates so he could keep a copy as his commission, while an elder sister and brother gave him shelter and meals; his mother died in his senior year.

Called on to recite: Dean Salonga would call him to recite precisely when student activities were at their height, testing whether he was keeping his promise never to neglect academics amid 'adulation for my leadership activities.'
Roces the Ninong: so impressed by the young dean's 'Education for Culture' campaign that he cultivated his friendship, made him NUSP adviser, and had him stand as Ninong at his 1961 wedding to Leni.

The chaplain who introduced him to God: baptized a Catholic but with no catechetical background, he was taken up by Fr. Michael Nolan, recruited into the FEU Student Catholic Action and taught the rudiments of the faith.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 12 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduced CJP's Far Eastern University commencement address, delivered as the university conferred on him the degree of Doctor of Laws, honoris causa. He opened with thanks to President Edilberto C. de Jesus and board chair Dr. Lourdes Reyes Montinola and with a joke that this second honorary doctorate finally made him 'the academic equal of my wife and children,' since he had been 'suffering from a venial inferiority complex' as the only one in his family without a graduate degree. Turning serious, he recalled his own 1960 graduation from the FEU Institute of Law, a father who was 'an underpaid but overworked government employee' supporting four children and seven siblings but who insisted 'education was the key to success and fulfillment in life,' and the deaths of both parents before he could finish -- a course rescued by an FEU scholarship and by his selling bibles to professors and textbooks to classmates. He then set out the four things FEU taught him. First, academic excellence: unable to afford 'the then 15-centavo bus fare' to UP, he enrolled grudgingly at FEU, found the faculty strict and demanding, and was driven by Dean Jovito R. Salonga -- who monitored his grades and called on him to recite at the height of his FEUCSO and NUSP leadership -- to graduate with honors and place among the bar topnotchers. Second, a well-rounded education, learned from Dean Alejandro R. Roces's 'Education for Culture' and President Teodoro Evangelista, from which he drew the legal corollary that 'excellence in law is not enough; a lawyer must also have a good grasp of the arts and sciences.' Third, his Catholic faith, given him by chaplain Fr. Michael Nolan, who 'introduced me to God,' and Fr. James Sheehy, and elaborated into a parallel between human, physical and spiritual laws. Fourth, a hunger for leadership, encouraged by Don Angel Palanca and 'Mang Etoy' del Rosario. He surveyed present FEU policies approvingly and closed with Salonga's teaching that 'it is far more important to aspire for the things that money cannot buy, like integrity, honor, dignity and a reverential regard and love for God.'
